Rubber trees from Brazil reached Malaya by way of Kew Gardens and Singapore in 1877; see rubber seeds leave Brazil. Henry Ridley of the Singapore Botanic Gardens worked out how to tap them without killing them and urged planters to grow them.

With the car industry booming after 1900, rubber spread over the western peninsula, and by the 1920s Malaya was the world's largest producer. Estates were worked mostly by Tamil labourers from south India, recruited much like the indentured workers elsewhere.

Malay smallholders grew rubber too. The crop paid for British Malaya, and its estates were a target in the Emergency. From the 1960s many were replanted with oil palm.
